A. Published Material
The regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(3) requires the Petitioner to submit "[p]ublished
material in professional or major trade publications or major media about the alien, relating to the
alien's work in the field for which classification is sought, which shall include the title, date, and
author of such published material, and any necessary translation." USCIS Policy Manual explains that
"[i]n evaluating whether a submitted publication is a professional publication, major trade publication,
or major media, relevant factors include the intended audience (for professional and major trade
publications) and the relative circulation, readership, or viewership (for major trade publications and

I
purportedly discusses "the company land [the Beneficiary]" satisfies this criterion,
maintaining that the publication constitutes a "professional publication."
I
The record includes an August 2021 Sport Aviation article that discusses the work ofl an
European engine company, and mentions that the Beneficiary was its chief operating officer (COO).
Even if we were to accept that the article, which only references the Beneficiary a few times, is about
the Beneficiary, relating to his work in the field of business, the record is insufficient to substantiate
the Petitioner's claim that Sport Aviation is a professional publication. Specifically, the Petitioner has
not offered evidence establishing the intended audience ofthe publication, or other materials to support
the finding that the publication qualifies as a professional publication. See 8 C.F.R.
§ 214.2( o) (3)(iii)(B)(3). As SCOPS noted in the decision, "[i]n response to the RFE [request for
evidence], [the Petitioner] did not provide additional information on the publication Sport Aviation."
The Petitioner's unsubstantiated statement on appeal that Sport Aviation "should meet this requirement
of being a professional publication" is insufficient to satisfy this criterion. As such, the Petitioner has
not demonstrated that the Beneficiary meets this criterion.

B. Original Contributions
The regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(5) requires the Petitioner to submit "[e]vidence of the
alien's original scientific, scholarly, or business-related contributions of major significance in the
field." USCIS Policy Manual explains that "[e]vidence that the beneficiary's work was fonded,
patented, or published, while potentially demonstrating the work's originality, will not necessarily
establish, on its own, that the work is ofmajor significance to the field." See generally 2 USCIS Policy
Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(2). Evidence that the beneficiary's work "has provoked widespread
commentary on its importance from others working in the field, and documentation that it has been
highly cited relative to other works in that field, may be probative of the significance of the
beneficiary's contributions to the field of endeavor." See generally id. USCIS Policy Manual farther
provides that "evidence that the beneficiary developed a patented technology that has attracted
significant attention or commercialization may establish the significance of the beneficiary's original
contribution to the field." See generally id. In short, the Petitioner must demonstrate that the
Beneficiary's contributions are both original and of major significance in the field of business.
On appeal, the Petitioner alleges that SCOPS "failed to understand the Beneficiary's] original
business-related contributions" and cites letters of support from the president of

The evidence in the record, including the above-referenced letters, does not sufficiently establish that
the Beneficiary has made original scientific, scholarly, or business-related contributions of major
significance in the field, as required under the criterion. See 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(5). The
l

impacted the field of business beyond his former employer or its clients. As SCOPS explained in the
decision, the Petitioner "did not include [sufficient] corroborative documentary evidence establishing
the significance of the [B]eneficiary's contributions." Similarly, while the Beneficiary was involved
with patents and intellectual property, the evidence fails to confirm that his work in the industry "has
provoked widespread commentary on its importance from others working in the field" or "has attracted
significant attention or commercialization." See generally 2 USCIS Policy Manual, supra, at
M.4(C)(2). As SCOPS explained in the decision, "[ w ]hile the testimonial letters were very
complementary ofthe [B]eneficiary, they did not describe how he made original contributions ofmajor
significance in his field." SCOPS observed that the letters "primarily spoke to the [B]eneficiary's
work ethnic and skill in business," but they did "not articulate how he made original contributions of
major significance in his field." As such, the Petitioner has not demonstrated that the Beneficiary
meets this criterion.

C. Critical or Essential Capacity
The regulation at 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(7) requires the Petitioner to submit "[e]vidence that
the alien has been employed in a critical or essential capacity for organizations and establishments that
have a distinguished reputation." USCIS Policy Manual explains: "[r]elevant factors for evaluating
the reputation of an organization or establishment can include the scale ofits customer base, longevity,
or relevant media coverage." See generally 2 USCIS Policy Manual, supra, at M.4(C)(2).
Additionally, the Policy Manual states: "[f]or a startup business, [U.S. Citizenship and Immigration
Services (USCIS)] may consider evidence that the business has received significant funding from
government entities, venture capital funds, angel investors, or other such funders commensurate with
funding rounds generally achieved for that startup's stage and industry, as a positive factor regarding
its distinguished reputation." Id.
